messages.subject: Permutation thresholds
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,
I realized that obtaining genome-wide significance thresholds are not
easily obtained in a 2-d scan.  I looked in the R manual to see how
R-qtl does it. I noticed that this was one of the recent major changes
in the software. Reading the manual I am still not sure how it is done.
Could you perhaps briefly explain or point me towards some literature.
In particular, I am not certain how to specify the NULL-model in the
scan. Suppose I want an 2-d scan between chromosomes (for which I have
already found some promising main effects) and the rest of the genome.
Ideally I just want the genome-wide null distribution for the parameter
estimating the interaction term. However, I think permuting the
interaction term alone does not make sense if I keep the the two
main-effect qtl vectors un-permuted. Similarly, if I permute the
phenotype against all of the terms (two main-effects and one
interaction effect) I would inevitably test: H0: qtl1 = 0, qtl2 = 0 ,
qtl1 x qtl2 = 0  versus H1: qtl1 > 0, qtl2 > 0, qtl1 x qtl2 > 0, but
this is not the test I want to perform.  What I want to test is:
H0: qtl1 > 0, qtl2 > 0 , qtl1 x qtl2 = 0  versus H1: qtl1 > 0, qtl2 >
0, qtl1 x qtl2 > 0.

Any help would be appreciated,
Regards,
Frank.

messages.subject: Re: Permutation thresholds
messages.body_plain:
Dear Frank,

Yes, it's not at all clear how to get thresholds for the 2d scan
results.

In a permutation test, one completely eliminates the effects of any QTL:
we look at the distribution of the genome-wide maxima of various LOD
scores,
under the global null hypothesis of no QTL anywhere.

But for the interaction LOD score, as an example, or for the "fv1"
and "av1"
LOD scores (which I currently prefer, and which indicate evidence for
a second
QTL), we would really want to know the distribution of these in the
presence
of a single QTL, not in the absence of any QTL.

And so I think we must hope that the distribution of the interaction
LOD score
in the presence of two additive QTL is the same as its distribution
in the
absence of any QTL.

I think the only alternative is to perform simulations: to simulate
data like
we'd seen, but for the case of just one QTL, and look at the
distributions
of the LOD scores in that sort of situation.

karl
